newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya cracks down on crime, hostage-takers.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya cracks down on crime, hostage-takers.

text.p: Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov, keen to improve his image and assert full control over his breakaway Russian region, on Monday launched a new drive against hostage-taking groups.

From early morning heavily-armed police, military and special forces brought together under Operation Shield of Law began stopping cars across the territory and demanding documents for any cargo in transit, police said.

Although the campaign, coordinated by the special anti-terrorist service, targeted all criminals, it was aimed especially at securing the release of five Russian reporters whose abduction has complicated the uneasy ties between Chechnya and Moscow.
Police said that by Monday afternoon they had already found two men wanted for murder.
Interfax news agency, quoting Maskhadov's spokesman, reported the operation had also freed six hostages, including two Chechens and two people from neighbouring areas of Russia.

Police said they were still combing the Chechen capital Grozny and other parts of the southern region for a three-member crew of Russia's commercial NTV television and two journalists from the Vzglyad news programme.
Taking hostages for ransom has become widespread in Chechnya, which was devastated by Russia's ill-fated 1994-96 military campaign to crush its independence drive.
Earlier this month, Chechnya won the release of a separate group of three Russian reporters, an Austrian businessman and a local resident held hostage by unidentified armed groups.

The rash of kidnapping prompted speculation in Moscow that Maskhadov, who won presidential elections in January after Moscow and Grozny had concluded a peace deal, was not in full control of his Caucasian territory.
Maskhadov denies such suggestions but has recently taken some steps aimed at asserting his control and neutralising potential threats from influential field commanders backed by powerful clans.
On Sunday he signed a decree dissolving the elite commando regiment Borz (Wolf), one of the most prominent combat forces during the 21-month conflict with Russian troops that ended last August.

Another decree issued on Sunday banned the self-styled army of field commander Salman Raduyev, who has openly challenged Maskhadov's authority and has complicated negotiations with Moscow by threatening terrorist actions in Russian cities.
Maskhadov, who led Chechnya's guerrilla army against Russian troops and then played a key role in the peace talks, is now trying to map out a long-term relationship with Moscow.

Under the peace deal, Russia has withdrawn its forces from Chechnya in exchange for a rebel promise to put off until 2001 a decision on whether the region should become independent -- the issue at the heart of their conflict.

Russia has ruled out Chechen independence and hopes that by 2001 it will have found ways to keep the region from seceding. Grozny sees the postponement as a chance to win better conditions in what it sees as an inevitable divorce.
Moscow and Grozny are now discussing control of a pipeline that runs across Chechnya and will deliver oil from Azerbaijan's new rich off-shore deposits to Black Sea ports.
To boost his negotiating position, Maskhadov needs to show he has enough control over Chechnya to ensure the safety of the pipeline.
